claims.claim: The prototype stopping at about 200 is almost certainly Tomcat's default limit of 200 worker threads, not a limit of Java or Spring
claims.why: The benchmark ran at 64 and 256 connections and never recorded thread-pool sizes or where a server stops accepting connections.

claims.claim: A few hundred requests per second is a small CPU load for one Spring Boot pod
claims.measured: java-spring on 1 CPU: 13,653 req/s plaintext, 27,264 JSON, 15,611 with 10 ms I/O wait; java-spring-vt: 20,006 plaintext, 14,571 I/O wait
claims.why: One CPU handled tens of thousands of simple requests per second, so a few hundred per second is a small share of one core.

claims.claim: With DeferredResult, 10,000 waits cost a few kilobytes each rather than 10,000 threads
claims.why: No async-servlet or DeferredResult setup was measured, and memory was not measured per waiting request.

claims.claim: Each request runs on a virtual thread that costs almost nothing while it is parked
claims.measured: I/O wait at 256 connections: java-spring-vt 14,571 req/s, 444 MB peak vs java-spring 15,611 req/s, 491 MB
claims.why: 256 connections cannot show the cost of each parked virtual thread at thousands of concurrent waits, and no figure per thread was recorded.

claims.claim: On Java 21, pinning of carrier threads in synchronized blocks can bring the original thread-exhaustion problem back
claims.why: The benchmark did not test pinning or compare JDK versions.

claims.claim: A different language (Go, Node.js, Rust, Elixir) would solve the problem but no better than Java does once the waiting is written asynchronously
claims.about: go-gin, go-nethttp, node-express, node-fastify, rust-actix, rust-axum, elixir-phoenix vs Java/JVM
claims.measured: I/O wait, 256 connections: go-gin 20,235, go-nethttp 18,905, node-fastify 17,462, node-express 14,188, rust-axum 21,042, rust-actix 20,772, elixir-phoenix 18,711 req/s; JVM async kotlin-ktor 21,766; blocking java-spring 15,611
claims.why: Even against blocking Spring, the other stacks were at most about 1.35 times faster, and the async JVM server (Ktor) matched or beat them, so the gap is well within a factor of 2 (though JVM memory was much higher).

claims.claim: Spring WebFlux / Reactor Netty is technically excellent for this, and the servlet stack is not expected to need it at this volume
claims.why: WebFlux and Reactor Netty were not among the servers measured.

claims.claim: Quarkus, Micronaut, Vert.x: their benefit here is small
claims.why: None of these frameworks were measured.

claims.claim: Tomcat's default max-connections is 8,192 per instance
claims.why: The benchmark did not record connection limits or test anywhere near 8,192 connections.
